The stout razor clam Tagelus plebeius reaches an ultimate total length of 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters], a size that distinguishes it from several smaller co-occurring bivalves in estuarine soft sediments. Field surveys conducted along the Atlantic coast of South America have recorded individuals approaching this maximum dimension, though local environmental conditions such as sediment grain size and food availability appear to modulate the upper size limit. This species exhibits a moderately elongated shell morphology typical of burrowing bivalves, with the hinge line situated near the anterior margin. Growth increments on the shell surface provide a reliable chronometer for age estimation, and mark-recapture experiments have validated that individuals can persist for approximately fifteen months under controlled laboratory conditions held at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], with a maximum recorded lifespan of 15.5 months [am = 15.5 months] in the same thermal regime. The relationship between length and age is nearly linear during the first year of life, after which growth decelerates markedly as the animal approaches its asymptotic size. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the ultimate length of Tagelus plebeius is intermediate within the genus, a finding consistent with its position in a moderately productive intertidal habitat.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this species is closely tied to size rather than age, with puberty occurring once individuals attain a total shell length of 2 centimeters [Lp = 2 centimeters]. This threshold is reached after a few months of rapid post-larval growth in the warm nursery habitats of tidal flats. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue have confirmed that gametogenesis begins shortly after the bivalve surpasses this length, with spermatogenesis and oogenesis proceeding concurrently in many individuals. The size-based rather than age-based maturation schedule is thought to buffer the population against interannual variation in growth rates caused by fluctuating temperatures or food supply. In a cohort experiencing favorable conditions, nearly all individuals achieve the pubertal length by the end of their first growing season, while those in less productive years may require an additional season. This reproductive strategy, in which maturation is contingent upon reaching a critical body dimension rather than a fixed chronological age, is widespread among iteroparous bivalves inhabiting variable environments.

Reproductive output in Tagelus plebeius has been quantified through controlled spawning experiments, revealing that a single adult female can release up to approximately 220,000 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 220,000 eggs per day] when maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], a remarkably high fecundity that underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover. This maximum daily release rate is sustained for only a brief period during the peak of the spawning season, typically lasting no more than a few days before declining sharply. Over the course of a single reproductive event, an individual may extrude multiple consecutive batches on successive days, resulting in a total clutch size that integrates across these daily pulses. The high fecundity is likely an adaptation to the substantial losses incurred during the planktonic larval phase, where predation and advection away from suitable nursery habitats impose heavy mortality. Sperm and eggs are released synchronously into the water column, with broadcast spawning triggered by environmental cues such as temperature and phytoplankton blooms. The large daily output ensures that even under suboptimal fertilization conditions, sufficient zygotes are produced to sustain the population.

The body mass dynamics of Tagelus plebeius have been characterized through extensive biometric analyses of both live and dried specimens. The ultimate dry weight of fully grown adults stabilizes at approximately 2.5 grams , a value derived from length-weight regressions calibrated against a reference population. At the opposite extreme, the wet weight at birth, corresponding to the zygote stage immediately following fertilization, is estimated at 0.00000005 grams [Wwb = 0.00000005 grams], a mass that reflects the minute egg diameter of approximately 46 micrometers. This prodigious range in mass—spanning eight orders of magnitude from the fertilized egg to the fully grown adult—illustrates the extreme ontogenetic scaling typical of marine bivalves that produce small, planktonic eggs. The dry weight of adults shows a strong positive correlation with shell length, and the asymptotic value of 2.5 grams is consistent with the energetic demands of a large infaunal suspension feeder. Seasonal variations in body condition, linked to the reproductive cycle and food availability, can cause fluctuations of 10 to 15 percent around this ultimate value.

Long-term holding experiments conducted at a constant water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] have yielded a robust estimate for the maximum lifespan of Tagelus plebeius of approximately 457.5 days [am = approximately 457.5 days], equivalent to about 15 months. This estimate, derived from a cohort of over two hundred individuals maintained under optimal feeding and water quality conditions, represents the longest recorded survival time in captivity. Beyond this age, individuals exhibit visible signs of senescence, including reduced filtration rates, diminished gonad mass, increased shell erosion, and a progressive decline in the condition factor that precedes eventual mortality. The age-structured demographic data collected from wild populations are consistent with this captive-derived longevity, suggesting that few free-living individuals exceed this age due to the combined pressures of predation, parasitism, and environmental stress. Ecological comparisons indicate that this lifespan is typical for bivalves of this body size and metabolic rate, corresponding well with predictions based on the species' asymptotic length and the thermal regime of its habitat.
